EU ministers to step up deportations in bid to deter refugees | Migration

EU governments are to attempt to come up with a battery of policies aimed at sealing off “Fortress Europe” from unwanted migrants and stepping up the speed and volume of deportations for refused asylum seekers.


According to 10 pages of draft decisions prepared for the session on Thursday, the European institutions and national governments are to make a show of deporting refused asylum seekers in what looks like a vain attempt to try to discourage others from making the journey.

The draft document speaks of €800m (£587m) being earmarked between now and 2020 for deportation operations. There is to be greater recourse to pressuring source countries of migrants in Africa and the Middle East to take people back, using development aid, visa liberalisation and political leverage to secure compliance.

There is also to be greater use of “reception centres” or refugee camps in third countries where refugees and migrants can be held while asylum applications are processed, and more resort to detention within Europe to prevent those who have their claims rejected disappearing within the EU.

In the midst of its worst migration crisis, the EU is desperate to come up with some quick fixes. However, senior diplomats in Brussels involved in preparing for the meeting of EU interior ministers in Luxembourg complain that their political bosses are demanding instant solutions that are not available.

The draft document states: “The EU and its member states must do more in terms of return. Increased return rates should act as a deterrent to irregular migration.” But it admits that EU regulations governing deportation from 2009 are more often broken than observed.

Europe’s record in expelling migrants who fail to secure refugee status varies across its 28 countries, but on average at least 40% are not compelled to leave, according to European commission figures. Officials working on the present crisis estimate that the figure has risen to 50%.

The scale of the current emergency is complicating the response, say the officials. “The logistical problems in returning 200,000 people are immense,” said one.

The ambition to fund and build holding centres outside the EU where potential immigrants are penned in also faces big problems. Turkey, the biggest current source of arrivals into the EU via Greece, is a case in point.

Brussels and Berlin want Ankara to sign up to a scheme where asylum seekers would be held in camps while it is decided who qualifies for refugee status in the EU. But 80% of the more than two million Syrian refugees in Turkey are not in camps, have a form of ID card and are relatively free to go where they like in Turkey.

“We won’t put them in any kind of camp,” said a senior Turkish official. “We’re not going to have hotspots or reception centres. We’ve refused that.”

Hotspots refers to a European commission proposal for centres where migrants are gathered, identified, registered and fingerprinted while their asylum applications are processed.

An estimated 370,000 people have crossed from Turkey into Greece this year, more than half the total entering the EU. The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, visited Brussels this week for talks on how to cooperate on stemming the flow. The commission then published a joint EU-Turkish action plan.

“The contents of this are not agreed,” said the Turkish official, who insisted the plan represented a European wishlist. “We see it differently from the EU. The EU is in a crisis and it wants things done very quickly. We don’t have the same urgency. And it’s basically money and nothing else that they are offering.”

Commission officials are in Ankara trying to hammer out a deal with the Turks, and the commission vice-president, Frans Timmermans, has signalled his eagerness to travel there to seal the pact before next week’s summit.

But there is little chance of this happening. Ankara has also agreed to a separate bilateral working group on the issue with Berlin, which expects to take in up to one million newcomers this year. The German-Turkish negotiations are reckoned to have a greater chance of success.
